gaps.sentence: The children ___ great fun at the party.
gaps.explanation: have fun / have great fun is the fixed collocation; 'made fun' means mocked someone.

gaps.sentence: I ___ hours yesterday trying to fix the printer, and it still doesn't work.
gaps.hint: fixed phrase: to use time without any result
gaps.explanation: waste time means to spend time uselessly; the second clause shows there was no result.

gaps.sentence: I'd rather ___ by card than carry cash.
gaps.explanation: pay by card/in cash is the fixed pattern for the method of payment.

gaps.sentence: I only ___ sight of the celebrity for a second before the crowd closed in.
gaps.explanation: catch sight of somebody/something means to notice them briefly.

gaps.sentence: All candidates must ___ the written exam in June.
gaps.hint: collocation with 'exam' from the candidate's side
gaps.explanation: take an exam (or sit an exam) means to be tested; 'give an exam' is not used in British English.

gaps.sentence: She ___ the world record for the 100 metres last year.
gaps.explanation: break a record is the fixed collocation for performing better than the record.

gaps.sentence: The roads were almost empty — the traffic was surprisingly ___.
gaps.explanation: light traffic means few vehicles on the road; its opposite is heavy traffic.

gaps.sentence: The neighbours ___ a loud argument in the garden last night.
gaps.explanation: have an argument (with somebody) is the fixed collocation for quarrelling.
